theptip 2026/11/02 00:17
I think there is a massive opportunity for this kind of feed disaggregation. Used to be the recommender and indexing of content was hard, now I believe we can likely build our own according to our own preferences.

Haiku/Sonnet (or even Jev) can do a lot of the filtering work to rank and extend an RSS feed list.

I think this gives us an opportunity to fully cut the cord from eyeball merchants who want us to maximally engage and therefore polarize their content.

The big remaining hook will be the social graph; I am interested to see how far the EU push for mandatory interoperability will go. Another angle I’d support would be mandatory pluggable standards for your own ranking algorithm, but it captures less of the win than full disaggregation.

tabs_or_spaces 2026/11/02 03:43
I did something similar, but with current youtube search results and not really stress processing on HN data. My technique was simply saving my search terms and topics, and then putting that under a crop and continually updating the results. Super simple, but resulted in such a better experience for YouTube videos for me.

I call it "re-algorithming" your data. Basically you're not happy with the algorithm of a product, then you use it's data and introduce your own.

It also seems like folks are tired of the youtube algorithm and want something different instead? I'm willing to bet that many sites and apps have this opportunity in them.

mettamage 2026/11/02 01:04
This makes me think that perhaps we should like have a social feed. If I, for exmaple, say that one of my friends I'd follow them. Then whatever they synchronize as a recommendation, I'd get in my feed.

So that's not a like they give but a separate "publish this into my recommendations for my friends" feature. Which would then show up in my feed and everyone that subscribes to my friend.

A pubsub system basically. Users publish, friends of said users (if they want to) subscribe, and then that's how they get content.

miki123211 2026/11/02 02:38
FB basically tried this (it was basically what the "Like" widget on websites was for). It was a decent-ish heuristic for its time, but it ran into the fundamental issue that the people you consider "friends", the people you want to see life updates from, and the people who like the same kind of content you do, are groups with some overlap, but they are not the same people.

You probably want to see the pictures of your cousin's new kid, but you don't care for her flat Earth content or crocheting videos.

It's still far cheaper, faster, and less wasteful to wash by hand. It's just that the technique required to achieve that is... controversial? It's definitely always so misrepresented you'd swear it's the "before" part of a 90s informercial shot in black and white with a frustrated idiot failing at a simple task before throwing their hands up and pleading that "there has to be a better way".

Dishwashers simply aren't used in places with water restrictions. Broke people don't have a budget for dishwashing detergent because it's less general purpose than dish soap. There are likely people who started using their dishwasher more or even suddenly bought one based on those rants. It jiggled the handle on consumer trends that otherwise rarely change, so I consider that "influence".

If he stuck to just explaining how they work instead of attacking people's way of living, it would have flown under the radar.
